k1167: Price isn't the only variable, and it isn't even the most important one for risk-adjusted returns. A finished new build with its occupancy permit (<s1>leje përdorimi</s1>) already issued is the best risk/reward combination in the market — the premium over off-plan buys real protection. Off-plan pricing looks 20–30% cheaper for a reason: no escrow requirement means that discount is a risk premium, not free value. Pre-2000 resale stock carries a different, permanent discount in seismic zones — the market hasn't forgotten 2019, and it prices accordingly. Villas in Lalzi Bay, Farkë and the Riviera sit at the opposite end: a genuinely scarce segment with real diaspora demand behind it, <s3>distinct from the apartment market entirely</s3>. Land is the highest-upside, highest-risk category of all — titles, agricultural-status restrictions and restitution claims mean it's not a category to touch without a lawyer doing the checking, not the seller.

k1185: The discipline that separates good investors from bad timing
k1186: The single most useful habit among investors who don't get burned here: before buying "under" a piece of infrastructure, checking whether it's actually funded and under construction, only announced, or already finished. A project that's running already has its price gains baked in — buying "for" the Big Ring or the Llogara tunnel today is buying after the fact. A project with financing closed and construction underway has a real, partially unpriced catalyst left in it — <s1>the Tirana–Durrës railway is the clearest current example</s1>. A project that's an announcement without a budget line — a second southern airport, most "Riviera del Nord" marketing — isn't a reason to pay a premium at all. <s3>Whether the broader market is worth buying into right now is a separate, honest question</s3> — this article is about who's buying and what they're buying, not about timing.

k1202: Property Tax in Albania: What You'll Pay in 2026
k1203: What property tax will you pay in Albania in 2026?
k1204: Three taxes and one deadline. Housing is taxed at 0.05% of fiscal value a year, roughly 3,600 to 10,200 lek for a 90 square metre Tirana flat. Selling costs 15% capital gains, and short-term rental income has been taxed at 15% since January 2026. Until 31 December 2026 you can revalue at 5% instead.
k1205: Under Law 85/2025 and Udhëzimi 5/2026, between 1 January and 31 December 2026 any owner can revalue a property to its market value and pay <s1>5% on the increase</s1>. Do nothing, sell later, and the same gain is taxed at the 15% capital-gains rate. Apartments get a further 1% per year of ownership knocked off. The application goes to ASHK by 31.12.2026 and the payment follows by 31.03.2027.
k1206: If you expect to sell in the next few years, the arithmetic is not close. If you have no intention of selling, revaluing raises your fiscal base and therefore your annual tax, so it is not free.

k1208: Housing is taxed at 0.05% of fiscal value, which is the zone reference price times the area. Commercial is 0.2%. An unfinished building whose permit has expired pays 30% of the rate, and the municipality can move any of it by ±30%.

k1240: What's Living on the Albanian Riviera Really Like?
k1241: What's It Actually Like to Live on the Albanian Riviera in 2026?
k1242: Every Riviera article talks about yield. Almost none of them talk about what a Tuesday in February actually looks like, or what happens the first time the water cuts out in August. This one is for the second group of readers — the ones planning to live here, not just collect rent from it.
k1244: Two towns on this coast have a genuine off-season economy: <s1>Vlorë</s1>, which runs a working port and a student population that keeps demand alive through winter, and Sarandë, which functions as the south's only real year-round town for the same structural reason — an economy that isn't purely tourism. Everywhere else tells a different story. Ksamil, Himarë and Dhërmi are built almost entirely around a summer season that runs roughly three months; outside it, restaurants close, beach clubs shut, and the population most of the marketing photos show simply isn't there. If year-round life matters to you, that distinction is worth more than any price comparison between the zones.
k1245: Water and power: the coast's invisible ceiling
k1246: Albania's electricity generation is close to 100% hydro, which means a dry year is a supply problem, not an abstraction — and there's no desalination plant anywhere on the coast, nor one planned. Summer water shortages are a routine feature of coastal life, not a rare failure: Sarandë and <s1>Ksamil</s1> have both had chronic seasonal interruptions and documented sewage-network breaks, and Vlorë's own 24-hour water supply project is still in its first phase, with real shortages reported through the 2025 season. This is the least glamorous fact in this article and the one that shapes daily life more than any of the investment numbers do — ask any developer directly about the water source and the treatment plant before you commit, not after.
